identity.title: What Preferences Can—and Cannot—Predict in Multi-Agent Online Learning

problem.claim: The paper studies whether a game's preference graph can predict long-run behavior under payoff-driven no-regret dynamics such as FTRL.

gap.claim: Outside restricted subgames, preferences may not suffice to characterize dynamically stable behavior.

contributions.claim: Shows that the pure-profile skeleton of every dynamically stable set is preferentially stable, meaning closed under profitable deviations.
Shows preferences fully characterize asymptotic stability for subgames, but constructs a three-player counterexample beyond subgames where preferential stability does not imply dynamic stability.
Introduces leaklessness, measuring aggregate payoff drift away from a profile set, and uses it to give a payoff-based condition for stability and attraction of its span.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish where preference information is sufficient—subgames—from the general case, and introduce leaklessness to restore a stability guarantee.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report a three-player game whose preferentially stable set has a dynamically unstable span.
The authors report that preferences fully characterize asymptotic stability for subgames.
The authors report that leaklessness yields a payoff-based condition guaranteeing that a set's span is stable and attracting.

narrative_sequence.summary: Relates preference-based solution concepts to long-run outcomes of no-regret learning through the game's preference graph.
Establishes that dynamically stable sets must have preferentially stable pure-profile skeletons.
Shows preference sufficiency for asymptotic stability in subgames.
Gives a three-player counterexample showing the equivalence fails beyond subgames.
Adds leaklessness as a payoff-drift condition supporting stability and attraction.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates a necessary implication, a restricted equivalence, a counterexample outside that scope, and a condition that restores a guarantee.

lessons.interpretation: Scope boundaries and failure cases make a theoretical claim more informative than an unrestricted sufficiency statement.
lessons.application: State a theorem with its exact domain, then include a minimal counterexample when extending beyond that domain and identify an additional sufficient condition.
lessons.exception: This pattern is less suitable when the work genuinely concerns only one narrowly defined setting and no broader claim is being made.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal definition of dynamic stability, the exact leaklessness condition, or the learning assumptions beyond mentioning FTRL and no-regret dynamics.
It does not report quantitative experiments, proof details, or whether the stated guarantees hold uniformly across specific algorithmic parameter choices.
